title: Review: Group 2; Group 1 reactions and group trends
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for Eduqas A-level Chemistry (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: PT09#t3 term and clue written for the game; PT04#t4 term and clue written for the game; PT04#t3 term and clue written for the game; PT09#t4 term and clue written for the game. Questions: PT04#N.9, PT09#N.5, PT04#N.5, PT09#N.2, PT04#N.14, PT09#N.8, PT04#N.15, PT09#N.9, PT04#N.7. The matching task revisits terms from the worlds it reviews, in a new mix. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Oxidising agent
items.clue: Role of a halogen, which reacts by gaining electrons: X₂ + 2e⁻ → 2X⁻.

items.label: Second ionisation energy
items.clue: Quantity for the change M⁺(g) → M²⁺(g) + e⁻, which falls down Group 2.

items.label: Oxidation
items.clue: Loss of electrons, as in M → M²⁺ + 2e⁻, where the state rises from 0 to +2.

items.label: Displacement
items.clue: A halogen pushes a halide lower in the group out of solution, e.g. Cl₂ with Br⁻.

questions.stem: Dilute sodium hydroxide is added to separate solutions of magnesium chloride and barium chloride. Dilute sulfuric acid is then added to fresh samples of each. Which observations are expected?

options.text: MgCl₂: white precipitate with NaOH only. BaCl₂: white precipitate with H₂SO₄ only.
MgCl₂: white precipitate with H₂SO₄ only. BaCl₂: white precipitate with NaOH only.
Both solutions give a white precipitate with NaOH and with H₂SO₄.
MgCl₂: white precipitate with both reagents. BaCl₂: no precipitate with either.

questions.explanation: Mg(OH)₂ is sparingly soluble but MgSO₄ is soluble. Ba(OH)₂ is soluble but BaSO₄ is insoluble.

questions.stem: How does the first ionisation energy change from lithium to sodium to potassium in Group 1, and why?

options.text: It decreases, as the outer electron is in a higher main level, further out and more shielded.
It decreases, as the fixed pull of the nucleus is shared among a larger number of electrons.
It increases, as the nuclear charge rises from +3 to +19 and attracts the electron more strongly.
It stays the same, as each atom must lose just one electron to reach a full outer shell.

questions.explanation: Down the group the electron removed is in a higher main energy level (n = 2, 3, 4), further from the nucleus and shielded by more inner electrons. This outweighs the rise in nuclear charge: Li 520, Na 496, K 419 kJ mol⁻¹.

questions.stem: Which equation shows the reaction of strontium with cold water?

options.text: Sr(s) + H₂O(l) → SrO(s) + H₂(g)
Sr(s) + 2H₂O(l) → Sr(OH)₂(aq) + H₂(g)
2Sr(s) + 2H₂O(l) → 2SrOH(aq) + H₂(g)
SrO(s) + H₂O(l) → Sr(OH)₂(aq)

questions.explanation: Sr forms Sr²⁺, so the hydroxide is Sr(OH)₂. Two water molecules supply two OH⁻ and release H₂.

questions.stem: A small piece of sodium is added to a large volume of water containing universal indicator. Which statement describes what happens?

options.text: Hydrogen and sodium oxide form, and the oxide stays as a solid
Hydrogen gas is released, so the solution turns acidic
Hydrogen and sodium hydroxide form, so the solution turns alkaline
The sodium dissolves unchanged, and the fizzing is air escaping

questions.explanation: 2Na(s) + 2H₂O(l) → 2NaOH(aq) + H₂(g). The sodium fizzes as hydrogen is released, and the hydroxide ions turn the indicator to an alkaline colour.

questions.stem: Which Group 2 carbonate decomposes at the lowest temperature, and why?

options.text: BaCO₃, because the large Ba²⁺ ion holds the carbonate ion only weakly.
BaCO₃, because barium is the most reactive metal in Group 2.
MgCO₃, because the small Mg²⁺ ion polarises the carbonate ion most.
MgCO₃, because Mg²⁺ carries a larger charge than the other Group 2 ions.

questions.explanation: Mg²⁺ has the highest charge density in the group. It distorts the CO₃²⁻ electron cloud most, weakening a C–O bond, so CO₂ is released at the lowest temperature.

questions.stem: Which mixture shows a colour change caused by a displacement reaction?

options.text: Iodine solution and aqueous sodium chloride
Iodine solution and aqueous sodium bromide
Chlorine water and aqueous sodium bromide
Chlorine water and aqueous sodium fluoride

questions.explanation: Chlorine is above bromine, so it takes electrons from bromide ions: Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂. The solution turns yellow-orange.

questions.stem: Strontium reacts more vigorously than calcium with dilute hydrochloric acid. The sum of the first and second ionisation energies is 1735 kJ mol⁻¹ for calcium and 1614 kJ mol⁻¹ for strontium. Which explains the difference?

options.text: Strontium has a larger nuclear charge, so it attracts H⁺ ions from the acid more strongly.
Strontium's outer electrons are further out and more shielded, so less energy is needed to form Sr²⁺.
Strontium chloride is far more soluble than calcium chloride, so the metal surface stays clean.
Strontium atoms have more electrons, so each atom can give more electrons to the H⁺ ions.

questions.stem: Calcium fizzes steadily in cold water, but barium reacts much more vigorously. Which explains the difference?

options.text: Barium has a larger nuclear charge, which pushes its outer electrons away more strongly.
Barium's outer electrons are further out and more shielded, so are lost more easily.
Barium atoms lose more electrons than calcium atoms, so each atom releases more hydrogen.
Barium is more electronegative, so it attracts water molecules more strongly.

questions.explanation: Barium's outer electrons are in n = 6, calcium's in n = 4. The extra distance and shielding outweigh the larger nuclear charge, so barium forms Ba²⁺ more easily and reacts faster.

questions.stem: Equal amounts of magnesium oxide and barium oxide are each shaken with water containing universal indicator. Which results are expected?

options.text: Both stay at about pH 7, because Group 2 oxides do not react with water.
MgO gives about pH 13 and BaO about pH 10, because Mg(OH)₂ is the more soluble.
Both give about pH 14, because every Group 2 hydroxide is a fully soluble strong alkali.
MgO gives about pH 10 and BaO about pH 13, because Ba(OH)₂ is far more soluble.

questions.explanation: More soluble hydroxide → more OH⁻ in solution → higher pH. Alkalinity increases down Group 2.
